L001.question: In the final paragraph the narrator concludes that her chief error at fifteen lay in:

options.A: asking after one graft, when the practice she was watching only answered across many grafts and many years.
options.B: assuming that the old varieties could be saved at all, a question the drought had already decided.
options.C: taking the skill for handwork when it was really a patience she did not have.
options.D: trusting the columns in the book over what the trees in the row were showing her.

L002.question: Passage B's handling of the trench measurement reported in Passage A is best described as:

options.A: accepting the measurement and taking it to confirm the layer account.
options.B: accepting the measurement but attributing the change to the grains instead.
options.C: rejecting the measurement as an artifact of how the geophones were buried.
options.D: accepting the measurement but denying that it separates the two accounts.

L003.question: In the tray experiment of paragraph 3, the two groups of trays differed in:

options.A: the kind of clay the eggs were laid into.
options.B: the total quantity of water each tray was given over the week.
options.C: the number of separate pours in which the same total of water arrived.
options.D: the number of eggs set into the clay of each tray.

L004.question: The author of Passage B would most likely describe an archive that screens a 1915 film colorless, silent, and at a fixed speed as:

options.A: making an interpretation that is informed but has not been documented.
options.B: restoring the evening rather than the negative.
options.C: preserving the film's instructions while performing them incorrectly.
options.D: faithfully presenting a thing no audience was ever meant to see.

L005.question: The discussion of the English pair rime and crust in the fifth paragraph functions mainly to:

options.A: establish that English has no pair of words able to carry the frost and the bread.
options.B: demonstrate that idiomatic English cannot produce a rhyme without sounding forced.
options.C: argue that the completeness of a version is the measure by which it should be judged.
options.D: show what Ozias had to give up elsewhere in order to keep a rhyme that carried the proverb.

L006.question: Passage A anticipates the kind of objection Passage B raises at the point where:

options.A: it grants that the silence of the dune in February is unexplained.
options.B: it grants that six seasons is a short record for a slow process.
options.C: it grants that its geophones went no deeper than two metres.
options.D: it grants that without an avalanche there is no energy to guide.

L007.question: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "traffic" most nearly means:

options.A: the volume of material passing through a channel over time.
options.B: the movement of vehicles along a route at a particular hour.
options.C: the act of carrying a thing bodily across a distance.
options.D: dealings carried on between two parties.

L008.question: The authors' phrasing in paragraph 7, including the sentence "We say may," presents the adaptive explanation as:

options.A: a possibility raised only so that it can be set aside.
options.B: a suggestion that the work reported here does not test.
options.C: a finding better supported in the field than in the trays.
options.D: a conclusion they accept but expect their readers to resist.

L009.question: The passage identifies all of the following as contributing to the porch's decline EXCEPT:

options.A: postwar builders' tight budgets and fast schedules.
options.B: the rise of planned communities.
options.C: the transformation of the street into a place people drove through.
options.D: a new focal point in the interior that demanded darkness.

L010.question: The passage suggests that when a town's grocery store closes, the pharmacy, hardware store, and diner tend to close as well because:

options.A: the grocer's vacant building depresses property values along the whole of the main street.
options.B: the closure signals to the town's other proprietors that the population can no longer support them, and they sell while they can.
options.C: the pharmacy, hardware store, and diner typically lease their space from the same owner as the grocery.
options.D: the grocery store generated the daily trips that carried customers past them.

L011.question: The narrator offers her aunt's placing of her initials in the margin as evidence chiefly that her aunt:

options.A: kept the book less for the trees than as a way of instructing whoever worked among them.
options.B: handled the narrator's failure by the one rule she used on her own, making it countable rather than remembered.
options.C: wanted the failures that were not hers marked as such, while sparing the narrator any reprimand.
options.D: had settled that the narrator would take over the orchard and so belonged in its record.

L012.question: The author of Passage A ends with the phrase "including, I remind myself, my own" most likely in order to:

options.A: admit that she has sometimes restored paintings to match her memory of them.
options.B: explain why she no longer tells people she is returning a painting to its original state.
options.C: concede that the letter-writers' version of a painting is as valid as the object.
options.D: count her own expectations among the things her duty to the evidence must override.

L013.question: According to the passage, the independent grocers most likely to have survived the period from 1990 to 2015 were those that:

options.A: owned their buildings and paid themselves very little.
options.B: reached agreements with their wholesalers to reduce the size of the minimum order.
options.C: were located in Plains states, where wholesalers accepted smaller minimum orders.
options.D: served towns whose residents did not already make a weekly trip to a regional center.

L014.question: The central claim of Passage B is that:

options.A: archives should present silent films exactly as the surviving negative records them.
options.B: since every projection interprets a film, an archive should interpret openly and on evidence.
options.C: the tinting and music of a 1915 screening can be reconstructed with certainty from the trade papers.
options.D: film restoration is harder than painting conservation because no single object is the film.

L015.question: The writer's stance toward Fane's 1912 version is best described as:

options.A: treating him as the most accurate of the three in every respect that can be measured.
options.B: endorsing the customary condescension, though allowing that the version was influential.
options.C: regretting that a version so stiff should ever have been printed at all.
options.D: crediting him with seeing something the others missed, while naming what the sight cost him.

L016.question: The main function of the fourth paragraph is to:

options.A: establish that a loss of five to fifteen percent can close a marginal store.
options.B: explain how site selection lets discounters go where supermarkets cannot.
options.C: present a disputed causal question and where careful research has landed.
options.D: qualify the third paragraph's claim that the discounters' arrival is a genuine improvement for some households.

L017.question: The author gives the figures "one household in three hundred" and "one in fifty" chiefly to establish that:

options.A: complaints came disproportionately from the largest households in each ward.
options.B: the rise in complaints is far too large to be produced by the rise in population.
options.C: the town's population grew more slowly than the assessors' rolls suggest.
options.D: most households in the town never complained, even in the worst year.

L018.question: The author calls the events of 1891 and after "the most useful passage in the whole archive" because they show:

options.A: complaints falling steeply once the monthly figures stopped appearing, with the board reading that fall as a verdict on the water.
options.B: the board's economies doing more for the supply than its publicity had done.
options.C: complaints continuing to climb after the figures stopped, a result the minutes omit.
options.D: the board restoring the column as soon as it saw what stopping it had cost.

L019.question: The passage as a whole can best be described as:

options.A: an account of the porch's rise, decline, and partial return, framed by one historian's view.
options.B: an argument that a facade shows how its occupants wish to meet the world, porch or garage.
options.C: a history of the porch that credits its disappearance chiefly to postwar builders' budgets.
options.D: an assessment of the revival concluding the new porches will be used once habits form.

L020.question: The first paragraph presents the three English versions as differing from one another in:

options.A: the edition of the Hungarian text each translator worked from.
options.B: their length, measured in syllables and in number of lines.
options.C: the degree of care each translator is said to have brought to the work.
options.D: the century in which each translator first learned to read Hungarian poetry.

L021.question: It can reasonably be inferred that the critics of the porch revival mentioned in the seventh paragraph believe that:

options.A: a porch of the specified depth is deep enough for chairs but not for the swings and rockers that once furnished it.
options.B: the required depth was set for appearance, not for use.
options.C: the developments copied the porch's form but kept the garage door out front.
options.D: building porches will not by itself produce the street life that filled them.

L022.question: Both passages would agree with which of the following statements about a booming dune?

options.A: Sound is produced only while grains of one diameter are present.
options.B: Sound is produced only while the sand is in motion.
options.C: Sound is produced only while the surface is drier than the bed below it.
options.D: Sound is produced only while the dry surface layer is growing thinner.

L023.question: The passage indicates that the two wards which do not fit the author's pattern are distinguished by:

options.A: a population that grew considerably faster than the town's as a whole.
options.B: an error in the hydrant numbers the Courier carried for them at first.
options.C: a supply drawn from a different source than the rest of the town used.
options.D: complaint records that survive for only part of the decade in question.

L024.question: As it is used in paragraph 8, the word "temper" most nearly means:

options.A: harden by testing it against opposition.
options.B: hold back from its strongest form.
options.C: bring to a settled and even frame of mind.
options.D: keep an outburst of feeling under control.

L025.question: As it is used in paragraph 8, the word "check" most nearly means:

options.A: a case that could have told against the account.
options.B: a restraint holding the population's numbers down.
options.C: a mark entered to confirm that a step was carried out.
options.D: a halt called to a line of work already under way.

L026.question: The authors of Passage A and Passage B would most likely agree that a restorer's decisions should be governed by:

options.A: surviving evidence rather than by what any individual remembers or prefers.
options.B: the rule that nothing be added that cannot be shown to have been the maker's own.
options.C: the public's attachment to the version of a work it has come to know.
options.D: the principle that the object a museum or archive holds is itself the work.

L027.question: The authors report results at three temperatures mainly in order to:

options.A: remove a second thing a first rain supplies as an explanation of the difference.
options.B: show that the beetle's range is limited by warmth as much as by water.
options.C: establish the temperature at which hatching proceeds most quickly.
options.D: account for the few larvae that the single-pour trays did produce.

L028.question: In the opening paragraph, the narrator characterizes her state of mind on the bus as one in which she:

options.A: grasped that she was being sent away and half-grasped that she was also being handed something she could not yet name.
options.B: had asked for the summer herself and regretted the request before the bus reached the river.
options.C: already knew she would spend her life among trees, and resented only the timing of the move.
options.D: expected the orchard work to be beyond her, and minded that more than she minded being sent.

L029.question: Paragraph 6 contributes to the passage chiefly by:

options.A: supplying background about the town on which the later paragraphs depend.
options.B: identifying a gap in the archive that leaves the question largely undecidable.
options.C: meeting a rival explanation with a record that the explanation cannot cover.
options.D: conceding a point the author cannot answer and narrowing the claim accordingly.

L030.question: The fourth paragraph cites Aird's letter to her editor in order to establish that what her version leaves out was:

options.A: given up knowingly, by a translator who could see what she was giving up.
options.B: something she came to regret, although she went on defending the version in public.
options.C: cut at her editor's urging, against a judgment she had already reached on her own.
options.D: absent from the Hungarian as she read it, whatever later scholars have found there.

L031.question: The "cumulative" account described in paragraph 2 held that an egg hatches once:

options.A: the clay around it has warmed past a threshold the dry season never reaches.
options.B: the pan around it has begun to hold water standing on the surface.
options.C: enough water in total has reached it, however that water arrived.
options.D: two separate rains have fallen within a few days of each other.

L032.question: According to Passage B, the collisions in a sheared layer begin to beat together because:

options.A: the steel floor of the chute reflects energy back up into the layer.
options.B: shearing sorts the grains by diameter into bands that move at one speed.
options.C: a grain striking early is slowed and a grain striking late is driven forward.
options.D: moisture between the grains binds them into clusters that move as one.

L033.question: The main purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: argue that community-owned grocery stores should be judged as infrastructure rather than as businesses.
options.B: compare municipal stores and cooperatives in towns without a grocer.
options.C: explain why rural grocery stores close and examine how towns have responded.
options.D: trace how small-format discount chains came to dominate rural retail and weigh the evidence that they cause closures.

L034.question: In the eighth paragraph, the writer grants that a version must succeed as an English poem chiefly in order to:

options.A: take up the strongest objection on its own terms and then show how little it decides.
options.B: concede that readers without Hungarian are not the audience the essay is written for.
options.C: withdraw the criticism of Aird made earlier and put Fane in her place.
options.D: establish that a translator's obligations end once the result reads well in English.

L035.question: According to Passage B, a silent film as shown in 1915 differed from its negative in that the film as shown:

options.A: was colorless and silent but ran at a fixed speed set by the studio rather than by each theater.
options.B: had been dyed by the archive that would later preserve it.
options.C: followed the studio's tinting instructions exactly.
options.D: was tinted, projected at a speed that varied by theater, and accompanied by live music.

L036.question: According to Passage A, the geophone measurements were what established that:

options.A: the booming face is a dry, loosely packed layer lying over a denser, damper bed.
options.B: the dominant frequency of the boom sits near 90 hertz on most afternoons.
options.C: the boom goes on for several seconds after the avalanche has stopped.
options.D: the sound is produced by a deliberately started avalanche and not by wind.

L037.question: The author's treatment of the disagreement between skeptics and advocates in the final paragraph can best be described as:

options.A: inclined toward the advocates, since the author frames the stores as infrastructure first.
options.B: even-handed, presenting the two sides as disagreeing about values rather than about facts.
options.C: inclined toward the skeptics, since the author grants that the stores fail as businesses.
options.D: even-handed, though noting that the electrification analogy rests on disputed figures.

L038.question: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that a tax abatement offered to a regional chain usually fails to attract a store because:

options.A: the forgone taxes are the revenue a town would need to finance a store of its own.
options.B: the abatement does nothing to increase the number of customers the store would serve.
options.C: regional chains, like the discounters, avoid towns whose grocers have already failed.
options.D: a discount store within fifteen miles would give the chain established competition.

L039.question: As it is used in the phrase "until recently, considered exotic", the word exotic most nearly means:

options.A: extravagant.
options.B: impractical.
options.C: foreign.
options.D: unusual.

L040.question: According to Passage A, the people who write letters after a museum cleans a painting are typically reacting to:

options.A: chemical shifts in the pigments that no solvent can reverse.
options.B: the museum's failure to consult records of what the artist intended.
options.C: overpaint by earlier restorers that the museum chose to leave in place.
options.D: the removal of a darkened varnish that had changed the painting's colors.

L041.question: The set of trays that received no first pour at all is significant because it indicates that hatching requires:

options.A: fresh water reaching an egg that has been sitting in salt, whether or not a wetting came before.
options.B: a total of water no smaller than the two-pour trays were given.
options.C: two wettings, provided that the second is fresher than the first.
options.D: an interval long enough for the clay to dry completely between wettings.

L042.question: The main purpose of the third paragraph is to:

options.A: show that the porch's unwritten rules were enforced by neighbors rather than by the household itself.
options.B: trace how a functional appendage became a room one was expected to sit in.
options.C: describe how the porch's physical features corresponded to degrees of social closeness.
options.D: explain why the front door, rather than the porch, marked the true boundary of the private household.

L043.question: According to the passage, the water board's own minutes for 1889 treat the rise in written complaints as:

options.A: a plain sign that the works supplying the town had gotten worse.
options.B: a change the board expected would reverse once the season turned.
options.C: a sign that residents had grown less willing to tolerate ordinary faults.
options.D: something the board could not account for from the records it kept.

L044.question: The passage indicates that the pore water surrounding an egg is far less salty at the second rain than at the first because:

options.A: the first water dissolved the crust and carried its salt down as it drained.
options.B: salt-tolerant growth takes up the salt in the interval between the rains.
options.C: the second rain falls on clay already saturated, so most of it runs off.
options.D: the second rain of the season is usually the heavier of the two.

L045.question: The paintings conservator quoted in the third paragraph of Passage B holds a position closest to which statement in Passage A?

options.A: The author can remove "what is demonstrably not the artist's" and must "stop there."
options.B: A museum "is a keeper of paintings," not "a keeper of memories of paintings."
options.C: "There is no such state to return to."
options.D: The letter-writers "are not wrong that something is lost when the varnish goes," and she takes that seriously.

L046.question: Passage B's description of the laboratory chute most strongly implies that:

options.A: a chute two metres long is too short to reproduce a full dune avalanche.
options.B: booming is louder in the laboratory than it is on a dune face.
options.C: the sand carried out of Al-Munkhafid is unusual among desert sands.
options.D: booming does not require the layered structure that Passage A describes.

L047.question: The writer argues in the second paragraph that Demeter's rhyme matters because the two rhyming words:

options.A: are the only words in the poem drawn from ordinary domestic speech.
options.B: are also the halves of a regional proverb, so that the sound carries the poem's claim.
options.C: occur nowhere else in her work, which makes them a signature of the poem.
options.D: supply the nine-syllable measure that the rest of the poem departs from.

L048.question: In the quotation from Ruth Ambler, the phrase "change the subject" is used to suggest that the disappearance of the porch:

options.A: reflected a preference for privacy over visibility.
options.B: made the automobile, rather than the street, the facade's subject.
options.C: shifted historians' attention from the porch itself to the backyard, the automobile, and the screen.
options.D: redirected sociability toward other settings rather than ending it.

L049.question: The authors' description of the salting experiment they have not yet run serves chiefly to:

options.A: concede that the tray work would be impossible to repeat on the Flats.
options.B: propose a use for the finding in settings beyond the Flats themselves.
options.C: name in advance the outcome that would defeat the explanation they have given.
options.D: explain why the ridge population cannot be studied under field conditions.

L050.question: In writing that "a thing nobody knows about cannot be a thing you failed at," the narrator presents her secrecy about the fence-line graft as:

options.A: a wish to try a method her aunt had rejected, which she admits was past her skill.
options.B: a way of sparing her aunt one more task in a season that was already hard.
options.C: a small rebellion that she now sees as the start of a practice of her own.
options.D: self-protection, rather than the deference to her aunt's judgment she claimed at the time.

L051.question: As it is used in the phrase "made the gradations legible", the word legible most nearly means:

options.A: firmly fixed.
options.B: socially acceptable.
options.C: easy to recognize.
options.D: readable as text.

L052.question: According to the second paragraph, Ceno set new scions into the old trunks mainly because:

options.A: the drought had killed the young trees she had planted in an earlier year.
options.B: the trees had grown too large to be pulled out without machinery she could not hire.
options.C: the packing houses paid her for scion wood cut from her older varieties.
options.D: the trunks themselves were still sound while the fruit they bore had no buyer.

L053.question: Compared with Passage A, Passage B places more emphasis on:

options.A: the duty to remove what later hands have added to a work.
options.B: the chemical changes that alter a work as it ages.
options.C: the reactions of the public to a restored work.
options.D: the restorer's obligation to make choices that the surviving material does not settle.

L054.question: The passage indicates that small-format discount chains can operate profitably in towns where a supermarket cannot because they:

options.A: occupy small buildings, employ few people, and stock mainly nonperishable goods.
options.B: arrive only after the local grocer has closed, so they face no competition for the town's volume.
options.C: locate within fifteen miles of nearly every resident, so that each store draws on several towns at once.
options.D: carry the fresh produce and meat residents would otherwise drive far to buy.

L055.question: As it is used in Passage A, the word "unforgiving" most nearly means:

options.A: allowing no excuse if it turns out to be wrong.
options.B: slow to be accepted by others in the discipline.
options.C: harsh in tone toward researchers who disagree.
options.D: demanding a great deal of labour in the field.

L056.question: The narrator's treatment of Mr. Baradas is best described as:

options.A: a correction of her younger view that allows his case its full force.
options.B: a defence of her aunt that grants he was courteous but not serious.
options.C: an admission that he had been right and that her aunt was merely stubborn.
options.D: a portrait of a rival whose motives she still finds hard to credit.

L057.question: According to the passage, hatching on the Menara Flats takes place:

options.A: within roughly two days of the season's second heavy rain.
options.B: only where several rains have fallen within a few hours of each other.
options.C: at intervals spread through the wet season rather than all at once.
options.D: as soon as the season's first heavy rain has soaked the pan.

L058.question: According to the passage, the porch's architectural ancestors served which of the following practical purposes?

options.A: letting air move through a house while keeping passersby at a distance from its doors.
options.B: shading the perimeter of a house so that its occupants could sit outdoors on hot evenings.
options.C: keeping sun off walls and keeping floodwater away from entries.
options.D: raising the entry of a townhouse so that its household could be seen and greeted from the street.

L059.question: The passage indicates that across the years in which complaints multiplied, the board's surviving sample sheets record:

options.A: readings that the clerk left off taking before the complaints peaked.
options.B: readings that improved on both of the measures the clerk entered.
options.C: readings too irregular from month to month to support any conclusion.
options.D: readings that improved on one measure while worsening on the other.

L060.question: As it is used in the third paragraph of Passage B, the word "alarming" most nearly means:

options.A: troubling.
options.B: surprising.
options.C: dangerous.
options.D: thrilling.

L061.question: The author cites the survey of twelve community-owned stores primarily as evidence that:

options.A: a subsidized store can produce benefits that its own ledger does not show.
options.B: a municipally owned store, unlike a cooperative, can be financed the way a town finances its water system.
options.C: the sample of community-owned stores is still too small to support conclusions about their finances.
options.D: residents of towns with community-owned stores shop locally out of loyalty rather than convenience.

L062.question: The passage indicates that before March 1886 the board's readings reached the public:

options.A: every month, but only in the board's own year-end report.
options.B: only when a resident asked for them at the counter.
options.C: once a year, and as one figure standing for the whole town.
options.D: not at all, the board having kept them as internal working papers.

L063.question: Passage A reports that the dominant frequency of the boom rose from 76 hertz to 104 hertz between October and March. Passage A attributes that rise to:

options.A: a decrease in the thickness of the dry surface layer.
options.B: an increase in the speed at which the avalanche ran.
options.C: a rise in the moisture content of the deeper bed.
options.D: a change in the size and packing of the grains.

L064.question: The examination in August established that the narrator's graft had died because:

options.A: the wrapping had been tied too loosely to hold the scion against the wood.
options.B: the two cut faces sat out of true, so that the living layers never met.
options.C: the tree at the fence line was too far gone to carry new growth.
options.D: the scion was of a variety that will not hold on that rootstock.

L065.question: The author most likely mentions the garage door in the final paragraph in order to:

options.A: acknowledge, against Ambler, that the automobile did more than change the subject.
options.B: identify the feature that now makes the facade's "argument" in the place the porch once held.
options.C: suggest that the newer argument the facade makes is, on balance, the worse one.
options.D: note that the house now addresses the street with a feature passersby rarely see opened.

L066.question: The test the writer proposes in the last paragraph is whether a version:

options.A: preserves the largest share of the original that its translator can be got to manage.
options.B: prints the original alongside it so that the reader may check the work.
options.C: reads so smoothly that nothing in it interrupts an English reader's progress.
options.D: lets an English reader feel the place where the original will not come over.

L067.question: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "spare" most nearly means:

options.A: offered without having been asked for.
options.B: kept in reserve against future need.
options.C: thin to the point of severity.
options.D: given in few words.

L068.question: The scholars who object that "changing the subject" understates what was lost would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: Ambler is right that sociability was redirected, but wrong about where it went.
options.B: Being visible from the street imposed a cost on households that the patio's privacy relieved.
options.C: The backyard patio hosts the same gatherings the porch once did, but fewer of them.
options.D: Unplanned contact between neighbors has value that barbecues do not.

L069.question: The narrator's account of the sentence her aunt repeated all summer serves mainly to:

options.A: show that her aunt applied a rule to the narrator's grafts that she relaxed for her own.
options.B: explain why the narrator asked fewer questions as the weeks went on, without giving them up.
options.C: concede that her aunt's manner was cold while maintaining that the coldness was earned.
options.D: mark a distinction she missed at the time, between refusing to guess and not caring.

L070.question: The author quotes a complainant who says the water at his tap is "worse than the sheet allows" mainly in order to show that:

options.A: complaints grew more restrained once a figure was available to be cited.
options.B: the published readings were frequently too low to be believed by anyone.
options.C: the households nearest the tannery had the strongest grounds for complaining.
options.D: the complaint now takes a published reading as the thing it argues with.

L071.question: Passage B calls the October-to-March trench result ambiguous. That charge depends on which further fact about the two visits?

options.A: A thinner dry layer avalanches faster, so the shear rate changed as well.
options.B: The grains were the same grains on both visits, so no grain property changed.
options.C: The frequency was recorded by buried geophones rather than at the surface.
options.D: The trench was cut across a single face rather than across several faces.

L072.question: The writer brings up Demeter's own translations of Ricour in order to show that Demeter:

options.A: believed a poem's season and its imagery were the parts least worth preserving.
options.B: was a stronger poet in Hungarian than the French poet whose work she was rendering.
options.C: took a translation to be a second made thing rather than a copy of a first.
options.D: had held a strict standard of fidelity before her own poems were translated.
